A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Group-MATES research despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Group-MATES pretraining results on DCLM and C4, component ablations, influence-model evaluations, and clustering analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional larger-model experiments, equal-compute comparisons, rollout and selection-ratio studies, and inference timing.

M1.justification: v1 trains on total influences of data pairs and bootstraps pairs using individual influence and similarity. v2 predicts conditional marginal influence along training trajectories, averages relationships to previously selected points, and bootstraps through conditional predictions. Its default length-10 rollout replaces the pair-based procedure; v2 Table 6 retains the earlier 1B result as the length-2 variant.

E1.justification: Both versions use DCLM pretraining data, FLAN reference examples, the same downstream task coverage, and the C4 experiment with nine evaluation tasks. The added 3B model and compute-budget experiments expand configurations within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds WebOrganizer to the DCLM 1B-1x comparison in Table 1, explicitly using its published results under the matching setup. The existing Random, Edu Classifier, MATES, and Quad comparisons and the C4 comparator set are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 2.8B-parameter, 55.9B-token setting and equal-total-FLOP controls that train random-selection models on additional tokens. It introduces rollout-length, selection-ratio, and inference-scaling protocols. HellaSwag's 0-shot and 10-shot labels also reverse in the detailed tables while baseline numerical rows remain unchanged; those label changes do not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: v2 adds equal-compute controls, rollout-length and selection-ratio sensitivity studies, clustering runtime measurements, and an influence-prediction ablation without relationship weights. It removes v1's oracle/model relationship-overlap analysis, repeated-bootstrap-iteration comparison, individual-influence approximation comparison, and clustering variance/correlation diagnostics. The education and mathematical case studies remain, relocated to Appendix C.8.

E5.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 5.3's statement that analyses use five data splits with means and standard deviations, although shaded loss curves remain. It also removes all per-task standard errors from the retained C4 Table 8. These are reporting losses; a reduction in actual run counts cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Under the revised method, main Group-MATES Core scores change from 0.23514 to 0.23362 at 400M-4x and from 0.30685 to 0.30747 at 1B-1x. The earlier 1B result survives as the length-2 ablation. v2 adds the 3B result of 0.36846, equal-compute results, and sensitivity and timing findings, while revising several diagnostic results. C4 accuracies remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal leave-n-out and leave-one-out oracle definitions and a Hessian-based influence-function derivation. Appendix A develops the trajectory-specific influence expression from SGD perturbations, replacing v1's brief presentation and independent-plus-interaction decomposition. Clustering complexity is also reformulated explicitly as O(Nn/d).

C1.justification: The central contribution of relational group-level selection improving pretraining and achieving a DCLM state of the art remains. v2 replaces the headline 10%/5% improvement statements with 3.5%-9.4% gains across three scales and adds explicit claims of up to 1.75 times fewer tokens and reduced total FLOPs.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving longer-trajectory modeling difficulty, diversity loss under aggressive selection, and efficiency under equal compute. Appendix D explicitly limits validation to 412M-2.8B models and identifies unresolved production-scale stability challenges. Conversely, it drops v1's specific difficulty with strong amplification effects and its educational-filter overfitting interpretation, while retaining the case-study explanations.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the pair-collection recipe with 20,000 trajectories and explicit rollout length and width. It newly specifies two pretraining stages, a 50% selection ratio, Z-score normalization, regression-weight initialization, and H100 80GB training hours, alongside 3B hyperparameters. It also adds a code-release link; repository availability was not externally checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including WebOrganizer, Data Shapley, Datamodels, and second-order group influence functions, while removing references including DOGE, DoReMi, and Gumbel-Top-k. Positioning emphasizes retraining-based oracles and approximating costly group selection, while retaining the principal distinction between individual and interacting group influences.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewritten across the abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results. v2 separates preliminaries from methods, organizes results around the speed-quality frontier, and reorganizes theory, case studies, experimental details, and broader impacts across expanded appendices.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws Figure 2 around trajectory rollouts, expands Table 1, and substantially reworks the bootstrapping and clustering figures. It adds token/FLOP efficiency panels and sensitivity tables, removes several diagnostic panels, and relocates the case-study and FLOPs tables.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument: Figure 3 and Table 5 evaluate benefits after accounting for selection overhead, addressing a gap left by v1's cost breakdown and principally equal-token comparisons. Larger-model validation and rollout/selection-ratio studies strengthen the method's empirical justification, while implementation and code-release information improve reproducibility. Removing standard errors, the five-split explanation, and the amplification-error analysis reduces transparency, but these losses do not outweigh the stronger controlled evidence for the paper's main contribution.
